cards.prompt: Convert a list of date strings into real datetime values. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: to_datetime() parses strings (or numbers, or mixed formats) into pandas Timestamps — the type that unlocks date arithmetic and the .dt accessor.
cards.whenToUse: A date column loaded as plain text (very common straight out of read_csv) needs converting before any date-aware logic works.
cards.commonMistake: Comparing date strings directly ('2024-01-06' > '2024-01-05') — it happens to work for ISO-formatted strings, but breaks silently for other formats.

cards.prompt: Confirm ts's date column actually loaded as a real datetime type, not text. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: A column that looks like dates but loaded from CSV without parse_dates will show dtype('O') (object/text), not datetime64 — checking dtype catches this immediately.
cards.whenToUse: Right after loading any file with a date column, before trusting .dt access or date comparisons on it.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming a column 'looks like dates' means it behaves like dates — only an actual datetime64 dtype gives you .dt and correct chronological comparisons.

cards.prompt: Extract just the year from every value in ts's date column. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: The .dt accessor exposes date components (year, month, day...) on a datetime64 Series, mirroring .str for text columns.
cards.whenToUse: Grouping or filtering by a date component rather than the full timestamp.
cards.commonMistake: Trying date_column.year directly — the .dt accessor is required; without it pandas doesn't know to treat the Series as dates.

cards.prompt: Extract just the month number from ts's date column. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: dt.month gives the numeric month (1-12) — combine it with dt.year when grouping across multiple years to avoid mixing e.g. two different Januaries together.
cards.whenToUse: Monthly aggregation or filtering, e.g. grouping revenue by month.
cards.commonMistake: Grouping by dt.month alone across multi-year data — every January (regardless of year) gets merged into one bucket.

cards.prompt: Get the weekday name (e.g. 'Monday') for every date in ts. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: day_name() spells out the weekday directly — more readable than working with dayofweek's 0-6 integers.
cards.whenToUse: Reporting or filtering by weekday in a human-readable form.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing day_name() (a method, needs parentheses) with dayofweek (an attribute, no parentheses, returns an integer).

cards.prompt: Get the weekday as a number (Monday=0 ... Sunday=6) for every date in ts. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: dayofweek gives an integer, convenient for numeric comparisons like filtering weekends (dayofweek >= 5).
cards.whenToUse: Numeric weekday logic, e.g. flagging weekend rows.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming Sunday=0 like some other languages/libraries — pandas uses Monday=0.

cards.prompt: Make ts's date column the row index, producing a DatetimeIndex. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: A DatetimeIndex unlocks date-based slicing (like partial-string ranges) and is required by resample().
cards.whenToUse: Any time-series-style analysis — rolling windows, resampling, or date-range slicing all expect dates as the index, not a column.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting set_index() returns a new DataFrame — the original ts is unchanged unless you reassign or pass inplace=True.

cards.prompt: After indexing ts by date, select every row from 2024-01-05 through 2024-01-07, inclusive. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: A DatetimeIndex supports partial-string label slicing directly in loc — no need to parse the strings yourself first.
cards.whenToUse: Pulling a specific date range out of time-series data.
cards.commonMistake: Trying this on a column that's still text (not a DatetimeIndex) — string slicing works completely differently there (alphabetical, not chronological).

cards.prompt: Generate 5 consecutive daily dates starting 2024-01-01. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: date_range() builds a DatetimeIndex from a start point plus either an end date or a periods count, at a given frequency.
cards.whenToUse: Creating a complete date axis to reindex sparse time-series data against, or generating test/sample dates.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting freq='D' is the default anyway — but being explicit avoids surprises if you later need weekly ('W') or monthly ('M') spacing.

cards.prompt: Create a duration representing 3 days. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Timedelta represents a span of time, the difference-of-dates counterpart to Timestamp — adding one to a date shifts it by that duration.
cards.whenToUse: Shifting dates by a fixed amount, or representing the result of subtracting two Timestamps.
cards.commonMistake: Trying to add a plain integer to a Timestamp expecting days — you need a Timedelta (or DateOffset), not a bare number.

cards.prompt: Shift every date in ts forward by one day. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Adding a Timedelta to a datetime64 Series shifts every value by that same span, element-wise.
cards.whenToUse: Computing a due date, an offset reporting period, or correcting a timezone/off-by-one issue.
cards.commonMistake: Adding a plain int (ts['date'] + 1) expecting 'one day' — that raises a TypeError; it must be a Timedelta or DateOffset.
cards.example: # every date shifted one day later, e.g. 2024-01-02, 2024-01-03, ...

cards.prompt: Format ts's date column as 'YYYY-MM' strings, e.g. '2024-01'. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: strftime() renders dates as custom-formatted text — useful for display or for creating a month-level grouping key.
cards.whenToUse: Producing a human-facing label, or a coarser text key to group by (like year-month).
cards.commonMistake: Confusing strftime (date -> string) with to_datetime/strptime (string -> date) — they go in opposite directions.

cards.prompt: Filter ts to rows with a date between 2024-01-03 and 2024-01-06, inclusive, using a Series method. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: between() works on datetime64 Series just like numeric ones — pandas parses the string bounds for the comparison.
cards.whenToUse: A date range filter that reads more directly than two chained >= / <= comparisons.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting between() is inclusive of both endpoints by default, same as for numeric columns.

cards.prompt: Which correctly resamples ts to weekly total revenue?
cards.why: resample() buckets a DatetimeIndex into fixed calendar periods (like weeks) before aggregating — it needs a DatetimeIndex, which set_index provides here.
cards.whenToUse: Downsampling daily (or finer) time series into coarser periods like weekly or monthly totals.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for rolling() when you actually want resample() — rolling computes a moving window over existing rows, it doesn't bucket into new calendar periods.
cards.example:
# date
# 2024-01-07    520
# 2024-01-14    580
# Freq: W-SUN, Name: revenue, dtype: int64
